strengths: The dataset introduces an interesting scientific setting for graph learning: spectral curves represented as spatial multigraphs with explicit edge trajectories. Preserving parallel paths and their geometry offers capabilities beyond conventional adjacency-based benchmarks.

The construction effort is substantial: 11.6 million static graphs across 1,401 parameterized families, together with temporal sequences and several useful subsets. Poly2Graph combines established spectral theory, accelerated root finding, and adaptive image processing into a potentially valuable scientific tool.

The manuscript provides extensive mathematical background, pipeline pseudocode, a package tutorial, and feature and training specifications. Benchmark results include three seeds, macro-F1, and resource measurements; permissive dataset and software licenses are also specified.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not establish the central claim that edge geometry and multiplicity are essential to the benchmark. There are no geometry-removal or edge-collapse ablations, geometry-aware or multigraph-specific baselines, or simple descriptor/image baselines. Appendix D lists edge features but does not explain how each backbone consumes them; standard GCN, GIN, and GraphSAGE do not directly consume arbitrary edge-feature vectors. Consequently, the reported results cannot isolate the proposed learning challenges.

All models are trained for only five epochs with a shared initial learning rate of 0.01, without reported tuning or convergence curves. Very poor results, including approximately chance-level GIN performance on HSG-topology, could reflect optimization or implementation limitations. The three-band, full-scale, and temporal datasets receive no benchmark evaluation, leaving major parts of the contribution unvalidated.

Extraction accuracy is insufficiently established for a dataset whose defining property is topology. Validation consists of visual checks on hundreds of polynomials, without quantitative geometric errors, topology agreement rates, or resolution/precision/threshold sensitivity studies. Appendix B.5 acknowledges missing branches and disconnected components, but does not quantify their prevalence or provide quality flags. Calling fragmentation intrinsic to spectral graphs is misleading when the described failure arises from numerical precision and thresholding.

The target-label definition is inconsistent. Equations 11–13 identify classes only through the presence of powers of z, whereas Section 4 distinguishes families by their powers of E and free-coefficient placements. The binary support definition therefore cannot distinguish all the stated multiband classes. The treatment of zero coefficients and identical spectra across nominal classes also needs clarification and a label-collision audit.

Random stratified splits sample the same two-coefficient grids within every family. They measure interpolation within a restricted synthetic construction, but no parameter-region holdout or near-duplicate analysis establishes broader generalization. HSG-topology removes isomorphic graphs only within classes, and its comparison changes class count, balance, and sample selection simultaneously, preventing a clean explanation of the performance drop.

The claimed million-fold speedup and 20–40-fold memory improvement lack a reproducible numerical comparison: no matched workloads, absolute timings, baseline hardware, accuracy matching, or component ablations are supplied. Describing the implementation strategy does not substantiate gains of this magnitude.

Several broader claims exceed the evidence. Appendix E establishes a possible association through nonunique Toeplitz decompositions, not a well-defined matrix fingerprint; an unordered multiset also loses factor order, which matters for matrix multiplication. Scientific discovery and inverse-design benefits remain prospective. Claims of being the first spatial multigraph resource or the only temporal dataset with class labels also require narrowing, since Table A3 itself lists existing spatial multigraphs and labeled temporal skeleton datasets.

strengths: The dataset addresses a meaningful representation problem: preserving parallel edges with distinct geometric trajectories. Its 11.6 million static graphs, 1,401 classes, and parameter-dependent sequences constitute a substantial resource.

Poly2Graph combines established spectral theory, accelerated root solving, adaptive refinement, and skeletonization into a useful automated pipeline. Rich node and edge attributes support alternative representations beyond the supplied benchmarks.

The paper provides extensive implementation explanations and tutorials, specifies permissive licenses, and reports baseline results across three seeds, including macro-F1 and computational resource measurements.
weaknesses: The experiments do not establish the central claim that edge geometry and multiplicity are essential to the benchmark. There are no geometry-removal or edge-collapse ablations, geometry-aware baselines, or simple graph-statistic and image-based comparisons. Appendix D defines 13-dimensional edge features but does not explain how each backbone consumes them; standard GCN, GIN, and GraphSAGE do not directly incorporate arbitrary edge-feature vectors.

Baseline training is insufficiently validated. All models receive only five epochs with a shared learning-rate configuration, without convergence curves or documented model-specific tuning. GIN's 0.2% accuracy and approximately zero macro-F1 on HSG-topology particularly warrant investigation. These results cannot distinguish intrinsic task difficulty from optimization or implementation shortcomings.

Dataset fidelity is not quantitatively established. Validation consists of visual comparisons on hundreds of examples, while Appendix B.5 acknowledges missing branches and spurious component fragmentation. There are no representative error rates, resolution/precision sensitivity studies, or measurements of topology preservation. Calling fragmentation intrinsic to spectral graphs is misleading when the described causes are numerical precision and extraction thresholds. This directly affects the credibility of the topology-filtered subset.

The split and label design require stronger validation. Random splits mix samples from the same two-coefficient grids, but there is no audit of identical or near-identical spectra across partitions or conflicting labels across classes. Removing isomorphic graphs within each class does not resolve these concerns. Parameter-region holdouts would better test generalization. Moreover, Appendix A's binary support definition of polynomial classes does not clearly encode the E-power distinctions used in Section 4.

The headline million-fold speedup and 20–40-fold memory improvement lack a reproducible comparative benchmark specifying matched hardware, problem instances, precision, accuracy, and absolute timings. Appendix B describes the acceleration mechanisms but does not substantiate these unusually large quantitative claims.

The universal-fingerprint claim exceeds the argument in Appendix E. Nonunique Toeplitz factorization establishes a possible association, not a canonical or information-preserving representation. Collecting factor graphs into an unordered multiset also discards multiplication order, which matters for matrices. No useful invariance, discriminative guarantee, or downstream benefit is demonstrated.

The demonstrated utility is substantially narrower than the positioning. Classification recovers synthetic polynomial-family labels; no experiment establishes usefulness for physical observables, inverse design, or another algebraic task. The largest static subsets and temporal collection are unbenchmarked. Broad claims of being the first multigraph resource and exceeding all simple-graph datasets in class diversity also need more careful qualification. Overall, the resource is promising, but its quality assurance and experimental evidence are insufficient for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The dataset addresses a meaningful representation-learning problem: retaining geometrically distinct curves and parallel edges rather than reducing graphs to connectivity and node coordinates. The spectral-graph examples illustrate substantial geometric variety.

The resource is substantial: 11.6 million static graphs across 1,401 generating families, with temporal sequences and several benchmark subsets. An extensible generator adds potential value beyond the fixed dataset.

Poly2Graph combines established spectral theory, batched root finding, adaptive refinement, and skeleton extraction into a useful automated workflow. The appendices provide algorithm descriptions, feature definitions, training settings, and package tutorials.
The initial experiments report three-seed results, macro-F1 alongside accuracy, and computational resource measurements. The manuscript also acknowledges extraction failures and limited benchmarking.
weaknesses: The experiments do not establish the central claim that this benchmark requires learning multiedge geometry. There are no geometry-removal, edge-collapse, or topology-only ablations, and no comparisons with simple graph-statistic classifiers or geometry-aware, edge-conditioned models. Appendix D defines 13-dimensional edge features but does not explain how each backbone consumes them; standard GCN, GIN, and GraphSAGE do not directly use arbitrary edge-feature vectors. Consequently, the reported results cannot isolate the value or difficulty of the distinctive representation.

Training is restricted to five epochs with a shared optimization configuration, without convergence curves or meaningful hyperparameter comparisons. GIN's approximately 0.2% accuracy and near-zero macro-F1 on HSG-topology could reflect optimization or implementation limitations rather than intrinsic dataset difficulty. The full, three-band, and temporal datasets are not evaluated, leaving major advertised capabilities untested.

Extraction fidelity is insufficiently validated for a dataset whose central content is topology. Validation consists of visual checks on hundreds of polynomials, without quantified topology errors, failure prevalence, resolution convergence, or sensitivity to precision and merging thresholds. Figure A4 explicitly demonstrates missing connections. Calling fragmentation an intrinsic limitation of spectral graphs is misleading when the described cause is numerical precision and threshold-based extraction.

The prediction targets are not consistently defined. Equations (11)–(13) encode only whether each z-power has a nonzero coefficient polynomial, whereas Section 4 distinguishes families by E-exponents and the placement of free coefficients. The formal definition therefore does not explain the 1,401 labels. The manuscript also needs an audit of cross-class duplicate spectra and ambiguous labels, especially when sampled coefficients vanish.

Random stratified splits of a shared coefficient grid primarily assess interpolation within generating families. No parameter-region holdout, symmetry-aware duplicate audit, or out-of-distribution evaluation establishes broader generalization. HSG-topology removes isomorphic graphs only within each class, and its simultaneous changes in class count, imbalance, and sampling prevent attributing performance degradation to any individual factor.

The claimed million-fold speedup and 20–40-fold memory improvement lack a reproducible performance comparison: matched hardware, workloads, numerical accuracy, absolute runtimes, and component-wise ablations are not supplied. These unusually large gains are important to the contribution and require direct evidence.

The universal-fingerprint claim exceeds the argument in Appendix E. A nonunique Toeplitz factorization followed by an unordered multiset of spectral graphs does not establish a canonical or information-preserving matrix representation; factor order matters, and spectral graphs need not identify their source factors. More broadly, applications to scientific discovery and inverse design remain prospective. The promising resource does not yet have sufficiently reliable validation and convincing task evidence for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper introduces a potentially valuable scientific resource: 11.6 million spectral graphs across 1,401 polynomial classes, retaining parallel edges and their spatial trajectories. This combination offers interesting opportunities beyond conventional graph classification datasets.

Poly2Graph integrates established spectral theory, accelerated root finding, adaptive rasterization, and skeleton extraction into a useful automated workflow. Providing the generator alongside the dataset could enable custom scientific investigations.

The evaluation includes eight GNNs, five static dataset variants, three seeds, and accuracy, macro-F1, throughput, and memory measurements. GraphSAGE's 54.6% Top-1 and 95.2% Top-10 accuracy on HSG-12M demonstrate learnable structure.

The appendices provide substantial mathematical background, implementation descriptions, training configurations, and usage examples. Preserving raw edge trajectories allows future work to revisit the reference featurization.
weaknesses: Dataset fidelity is insufficiently established for a contribution centered on graph topology. Validation consists primarily of visual comparisons on hundreds of polynomials, while Appendix C.6 acknowledges missing low-DOS edges and fragmented components. There are no quantitative topology-error rates, resolution/precision convergence studies, or sensitivity analyses for thresholding and node merging. These errors could directly contaminate the topology subset and classification signals; Appendix H incorrectly characterizes numerical fragmentation as intrinsic to the spectral graph itself.

The experiments do not establish that spatial multi-edge modeling is necessary. GINE versus GIN changes access to geometric and physical edge attributes simultaneously, and the strongest baseline, standard GraphSAGE, does not directly consume those edge attributes. Missing controls include collapsed-edge graphs, multiplicity-only inputs, removal of potential/DOS features, geometry-only models, and simple pooled-feature classifiers. Consequently, the claimed irreducible contribution of multi-edge geometry remains unverified.

The training protocol is too limited to support strong conclusions about model capability or benchmark difficulty. Training stops after 1,000 steps with batch size 6,000, corresponding to roughly one pass or less through the full training set depending on distributed-batch semantics. There are no convergence curves, training-budget sweeps, or meaningful model-specific optimization studies. Matching parameter counts does not resolve this issue, particularly given GIN's poor and relatively variable results.

Stratified random splits across a fixed, densely sampled two-coefficient grid primarily test interpolation within known generating families. The paper does not audit geometric duplicates, symmetry-related samples, or cross-class spectral ambiguities across splits. Parameter-region holdouts and out-of-distribution coefficient tests are needed before interpreting the results as robust Hamiltonian inference.

Scientific utility is asserted more broadly than demonstrated. Polynomial monomial support does not uniquely determine a microscopic hopping pattern, as Appendix B itself explains. Only two coefficients vary within a restricted set of polynomial templates, so claims of covering all realistic systems are unsupported. No downstream inverse-design example, coefficient recovery, or physical validation establishes the practical value of Top-10 family retrieval. The temporal collection also has no evaluated task or baseline.

The claimed universal canonical matrix fingerprint is not justified. Appendix F acknowledges nonunique Toeplitz decompositions, but choosing a smallest multiset does not establish uniqueness among minimum-size decompositions. Furthermore, a multiset discards factor order even though matrix multiplication is noncommutative. The construction supplies possible graph representations, not the claimed canonical signature.

The reported five-orders-of-magnitude acceleration is insufficiently controlled. Table A3 measures only spectral-potential calculation, without enough hardware, backend, precision, matched-resolution, or accuracy information to assess comparability. End-to-end extraction timings and quantitative memory comparisons are also missing. The engineering contribution is promising, but the headline performance claim exceeds the presented evidence.

strengths: The dataset addresses a potentially useful and underexplored setting: spatial multigraphs that retain continuous edge geometry. The 11.6 million static graphs across 1,401 polynomial classes provide substantial scale, alongside sequences of parameter-dependent graph evolution.

Poly2Graph offers a practical engineering contribution by integrating spectral-potential computation, adaptive refinement, skeletonization, and graph extraction into an automated pipeline. Preserving edge coordinate sequences makes the resource useful beyond the proposed summary features.

The paper provides extensive mathematical background, generation details, package tutorials, and training configurations. Eight GNN baselines across five static variants, with three seeds and several metrics, establish an initial empirical reference.
weaknesses: Dataset fidelity is insufficiently established for a benchmark whose central value is topology and geometry. Validation consists primarily of visual inspection of hundreds of polynomials, while Appendix C.6 and Figure A4 explicitly show missing branches and spurious disconnections. There are no quantitative topology-error rates, resolution/precision convergence studies, or estimates of the affected dataset fraction. Calling fragmentation an intrinsic limitation of spectral graphs in Appendix H obscures its numerical origin. These errors could directly contaminate the topology subset and learned classification signals.

The experiments do not establish that retaining multiedge geometry is essential. There are no controlled comparisons against collapsed multigraphs, topology-only inputs, geometry-only inputs, or removal of potential/DOS attributes, and no baseline processes the full edge curves. GINE versus GIN changes access to several attributes simultaneously, so its improvement cannot specifically demonstrate the value of geometric detail or edge multiplicity. Moreover, edge-agnostic GraphSAGE performs best, and GINE does not outperform GIN on the one-band subset despite the claim of consistent superiority.

The evaluation measures random-split interpolation within a restricted synthetic generator. Every class uses the same coefficient grid with only two free coefficients, and Appendix E.2 uses stratified random splits. There is no coefficient-region holdout, extrapolation test, or audit of identical or nearly identical spectra across splits and labels. Consequently, the results provide limited evidence of generalization to new physical systems or practical Hamiltonian inference. The temporal resource receives no experimental evaluation.

The 1,000-step training cap, common optimizer settings, and parameter-count matching do not establish adequately optimized baseline performance. No convergence curves or budget-sensitivity experiments distinguish representational limitations from undertraining, particularly for the large datasets and poorly performing GIN. The conclusions about architectural suitability and the source of benchmark difficulty therefore remain tentative.

The physical interpretation of the labels is overstated. Characteristic-polynomial support is not generally equivalent to a unique microscopic hopping pattern; Appendix B.3.1 itself explains that determinant terms encode composite paths and cancellations. No downstream reconstruction or physical verification demonstrates that retrieving these synthetic classes enables material design. Claims that the restricted sampling covers all realistic cases are also unsupported.

The universal-fingerprint claim is not justified. Appendix F acknowledges nonunique Toeplitz decompositions but then asserts that a smallest multiset supplies a canonical signature without defining or proving uniqueness. Discarding factor order also loses information because matrix multiplication is noncommutative. Existence of a graph encoding does not establish a canonical, discriminative, or useful fingerprint for arbitrary matrices.

The reported speedup exceeding 100,000 times concerns only spectral-potential computation against one prior implementation, rather than the complete extraction pipeline. Appendix C.5 does not adequately specify matched hardware, precision, resolution, and output accuracy or isolate the contribution of each optimization. This limits the reproducibility and interpretation of a prominently advertised result.

strengths: The dataset targets an interesting, underrepresented setting: spatial multigraphs with explicit edge trajectories, grounded in non-Hermitian spectral physics. Preserving parallel-edge geometry gives it potential value beyond conventional graph-classification benchmarks.
The scale is substantial: 11.6 million static graphs across 1,401 classes, accompanied by temporal sequences and several useful subsets.

Poly2Graph integrates spectral-potential computation, adaptive refinement, skeletonization, and graph extraction into a practical automated pipeline. The generator is potentially a valuable scientific contribution independently of the benchmark.

The manuscript provides extensive mathematical background, implementation tutorials, training configurations, and three-seed results for eight GNN baselines. The stated permissive licenses support future reuse.
weaknesses: Dataset fidelity is insufficiently established for a resource whose central contribution is graph topology and geometry. Validation consists primarily of visual checks on hundreds of polynomials. The acknowledged fragmentation failures can change connectivity, while thresholding and node merging can remove genuine features. There are no quantitative topology-error rates, representative dataset-wide audits, or resolution/precision/tolerance sensitivity studies establishing that these errors are rare.

The training protocol substantially limits the benchmark conclusions. Appendix E.2 caps training at 1,000 steps with batch size 6,000, amounting to roughly one pass or less through the full training set depending on distributed-batch semantics. Without convergence curves, longer-budget comparisons, or meaningful optimization tuning, poor accuracy and model rankings cannot reliably be attributed to spatial-multigraph difficulty.

The experiments do not isolate the claimed importance of parallel edges and continuous geometry. GIN versus GINE changes access to several attributes simultaneously, including spectral potential and DOS. Controlled edge-collapse, geometry-removal, and spectral-feature ablations are missing, as are simple graph-statistics baselines and methods that encode full edge trajectories. The best-performing baseline is GraphSAGE, which further complicates the proposed interpretation.

Random stratified splits over a fixed two-coefficient grid primarily evaluate interpolation within the generator's sampled families. There are no held-out coefficient regions, broader coefficient variation, or audits of equivalent spectra across splits and labels. Consequently, the results provide limited evidence for robust Hamiltonian inference or materials-design utility.

Several major advertised capabilities remain untested. The temporal collection has no temporal benchmark, and inverse-design relevance is supported only by classification Top-k accuracy, without recovering or validating candidate Hamiltonians. Restricting most coefficients and varying only two also does not establish the asserted coverage of all realistic cases.

Appendix F does not establish a canonical universal fingerprint for matrices. Existence of a Toeplitz factorization does not imply uniqueness of a minimum-size factorization or its associated graph multiset; discarding factor order also discards information about a generally noncommutative product. These claims require a precise construction and proof or substantial qualification.

The headline speedup is incompletely substantiated: Table A3 measures spectral-potential computation rather than end-to-end extraction and does not adequately specify matched hardware, resolution, precision, and accuracy conditions. Overall, the promising resource is not yet supported by sufficiently reliable quality assurance and evaluation for acceptance at a selective AI conference.
